Title: BadAgent: Inserting and Activating Backdoor Attacks in LLM Agents
Abstract: With the prosperity of large language models (LLMs), powerful LLM-based intelligent agents have been developed to provide customized services with a set of user-defined tools. State-of-the-art methods for constructing LLM agents adopt trained LLMs and further fine-tune them on data for the agent task. However, we show that such methods are vulnerable to our proposed backdoor attacks named Bad Agent on various agent tasks, where a backdoor can be embedded by fine-tuning on the backdoor data. At test time, the attacker can manipulate the deployed LLM agents to execute harmful operations by showing the trigger in the agent input or environment. To our surprise, our proposed attack methods are extremely robust even after fine-tuning on trustworthy data. Though backdoor attacks have been studied extensively in natural language processing, to the best of our knowledge, we could be the first to study them on LLM agents that are more dangerous due to the permission to use external tools. Our work demonstrates the clear risk of constructing LLM agents based on untrusted LLMs or data. Our code is public at https://github.com/DPam K/Bad Agent
Major_Contribution_Result: BadAgent embeds backdoors into tool-using LLM agents by fine-tuning on poisoned agent-task data, with active triggers in user input and passive triggers in the environment. Across OS, WebShop, and Mind2Web tasks with AdaLoRA/QLoRA on models up to AgentLM-13B, the paper reports attack success rates over 85% on backdoor tests while clean-data follow-step ratios remain close to unattacked agents. The authors further report that the backdoor remains robust under fine-tuning on trustworthy data and under two data-centric defenses they evaluate.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: Due to training cost, the paper only reports agents with at most 13B parameters and only three agent tasks; larger models or other tasks may behave differently. The authors also state that, despite robustness against two data-centric defenses, it is uncertain whether effective defenses exist, and they leave stronger defense development to future work.
Critics: BadAgent evaluates fine-tuning backdoors on a narrow set of agent tasks and model sizes, focusing on attack feasibility rather than comprehensive defense benchmarking. Clean-task metrics (FSR) are reported alongside ASR, but the study does not establish a release-gate style agent-security evaluation process. Treat results as evidence of fine-tuning supply-chain risk under the paper's PEFT settings, not as a complete agent-security standard.
